title: Computing TCP's Retransmission Timer
summary: Defines the algorithm TCP senders must use to work out how long to wait for an acknowledgment before resending data. It expands on guidance in RFC 1122 and raises support for the algorithm from SHOULD to MUST. It replaced RFC 2988.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP resends data when an acknowledgement does not arrive before its timer expires. RFC 6298 sets out how a sender calculates that timer from measured round-trip times and responds when it expires.

questions: how does tcp compute retransmission timeout
how does tcp compute the retransmission timeout
what is the initial rto in tcp
subtitle: The rules TCP senders use to estimate how long to wait before retransmitting data.

tldr.problem: TCP needs a wait time before resending unacknowledged data. Waiting too briefly can cause unnecessary retransmissions, while waiting too long delays recovery.
tldr.mechanism: The sender estimates a smoothed round-trip time and its variation, computes the retransmission timeout, and doubles it after each timer expiry.
tldr.outcome: Support for the algorithm becomes a MUST, and the initial RTO is reduced to 1 second with a fallback to 3 seconds after a lost SYN exchange. RFC 6298 obsoletes RFC 2988 and updates RFC 1122.

facts.label: Backoff
facts.value: Double RTO after each timer expiry

today: RFC 6298 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2011. It obsoletes RFC 2988, updates RFC 1122, and is not listed as updated or obsoleted by a later RFC in the unit metadata.

sections.title: TCP's Retransmission Timeout
sections.content:
TCP uses a retransmission timer when it receives no feedback from the receiver. The timer duration is called the retransmission timeout, or RTO.

RFC 6298 formalizes the calculation described by RFC 1122 and raises support for the algorithm from SHOULD to MUST. It does not change the behavior TCP uses after the timer expires; that behavior is specified by RFC 5681. A sender may be more conservative, but it MUST NOT be more aggressive than this algorithm permits.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP starts a timer when data needs an acknowledgement. If the timer runs out first, TCP resends data that remains unacknowledged.

sections.title: Estimating the RTO
sections.content:
The sender tracks SRTT, a smoothed round-trip time, and RTTVAR, the variation in round-trip measurements. Before it has a measurement, it SHOULD use an RTO of 1 second. With the first measurement R, it sets SRTT = R, RTTVAR = R/2, and computes RTO = SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR), where K = 4 and G is clock granularity.

For later measurements, the sender updates RTTVAR using the old SRTT, then updates SRTT. The recommended values are alpha = 1/8 and beta = 1/4. Whenever a computed RTO is below 1 second, it SHOULD be rounded up to 1 second. An implementation MAY set a maximum, but that maximum must be at least 60 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP combines its recent travel-time estimate with a measure of how much that time varies. It keeps the result at or above 1 second, unless the recommendation changes in later research.

sections.title: Choosing Round-Trip Samples
sections.content:
TCP MUST use Karn's algorithm: it MUST NOT measure a round trip using a segment that was retransmitted. The sender cannot know whether an acknowledgement refers to the first transmission or a later one.

The exception is when TCP timestamps remove that ambiguity. TCP MUST take at least one round-trip measurement per round trip unless Karn's algorithm prevents it. With timestamps, each acknowledgement can provide a sample.
sections.plainLanguage: An acknowledgement after a retransmission does not show which copy arrived. TCP skips that timing sample unless a timestamp identifies the acknowledged transmission.

sections.title: Clock Precision
sections.content:
The RFC does not set a required clock granularity. If the variation term in the RTO formula is zero, the calculation uses at least the clock granularity G.

The RFC reports that clock granularities of 100 milliseconds or less perform somewhat better than coarser clocks. It also notes that techniques for improving precision with coarse timers are widely implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm uses the sender's clock precision when it calculates the timeout. Finer clock steps can measure round-trip changes more accurately.

sections.title: Starting, Expiring and Restarting the Timer
sections.content:
A segment MUST NOT be retransmitted less than one RTO after its previous transmission. The recommended management starts the timer when data is sent and no timer is running, stops it when all outstanding data is acknowledged, and restarts it when an acknowledgement covers new data.

When the timer expires, TCP retransmits the earliest unacknowledged segment, doubles the RTO, and restarts the timer using that doubled value. If the timer expires while TCP awaits an acknowledgement for a SYN and the RTO is below 3 seconds, the RTO MUST be set to 3 seconds when data transmission begins.
sections.plainLanguage: When the timer expires, TCP resends the earliest unacknowledged segment and doubles the next wait. If the initial connection request times out with a shorter timer, TCP uses 3 seconds when data transfer begins.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2988
sections.content:
The initial RTO changes from 3 seconds to 1 second. If a SYN or its acknowledgement is lost, the RTO returns to 3 seconds before data transmission begins.

The RFC's appendix explains this choice as a balance between faster recovery and avoiding unnecessary retransmissions. It describes measurements where more than 97.5% of observed connections had round-trip times below 1 second, while some connections had longer times.
sections.plainLanguage: The initial wait is shorter than in RFC 2988, so TCP can retry sooner when a connection request is lost. The RFC restores a 3-second timeout for data transfer after a SYN timeout.

viz.caption: RTO calculation rules from RFC 6298, Section 2

data.title: RTO calculation
data.code:
First measurement R:
  SRTT   <- R
  RTTVAR <- R/2
  RTO    <- SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR)  (K = 4)

Later measurement R':
  RTTVAR <- (1 - beta) * RTTVAR + beta * |SRTT - R'|
  SRTT   <- (1 - alpha) * SRTT + alpha * R'
  RTO    <- SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR)

alpha = 1/8, beta = 1/4
